status: completed relevance and independent occurrence-evidence review

review.requirement_proposition: Appropriate mechanisms should allow AI systems risking undue harm or exhibiting unwanted behaviour to be safely overridden, repaired or decommissioned as needed.
review.reason_for_change: The unwanted access/service behaviour directly engages the OECD repair proposition. OpenAI reported authentication recovery by about 08:20 PDT and full ChatGPT metric recovery by 09:00, corroborated by falling outage reports. This affirmatively supports repair in the reported restoration stage, bounded to the disclosed affected scope. It does not establish prevention of recurrence, full internal controls or every individual user outcome.

review.requirement_proposition: Use documented restrictive degradation rules when governance infrastructure is unavailable or indeterminate, and halt completely on governance-baseline integrity failure; block elevated-risk operations until governance is restored and verified.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: SDOS SDOS-EN-03 governs restrictive degradation of framework-governed agent runtime: Use documented restrictive degradation rules when governance infrastructure is unavailable or indeterminate, and halt completely on governance-baseline integrity failure; block elevated-risk operations until governance is restored and verified. The provider postmortem identifies overload amplified by retry/cache/routing behavior and backend availability errors unnecessarily triggering login flows. The record does not establish an SDOS undertaking, unavailable governance infrastructure, indeterminate policy or governance-baseline integrity failure. Authentication overload, plan messaging and partial component loss do not independently establish those framework triggers or prescribed recovery checks. Applicability remains unresolved without converting outage response into SDOS conformance.

review.reason_for_change: SDOS v1.10 was published after this April 2026 occurrence. The later restrictive-governance-degradation requirement is excluded on timing.

review.requirement_proposition: Establish and maintain communication plans to inform AI stakeholders as part of the deactivation or disengagement process of a specific GAI system (including for open-source models) or context of use, including reasons, workarounds, user access removal, alternative processes, contact information, etc.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: NIST AI 600-1 MG-2.4-001 concerns a voluntary GAI deactivation/disengagement communication plan: Establish and maintain communication plans to inform AI stakeholders as part of the deactivation or disengagement process of a specific GAI system (including for open-source models) or context of use, including reasons, workarounds, user access removal, alternative processes, contact information, etc. The provider postmortem identifies overload amplified by retry/cache/routing behavior and backend availability errors unnecessarily triggering login flows. The status report, workaround or upgrade suggestion does not establish adoption/selection of this Profile action or a source-defined deactivation/disengagement process and plan. Service outages and plan-capacity messaging are distinct from this prescribed procedure. Applicability remains unresolved; communication of an incident is not proof that the complete action was fulfilled or breached.

review.reason_for_change: An overloaded authentication-edge dependency reduced ChatGPT and related login availability, with ordinary availability errors unnecessarily triggering login. Loss of the operational GAI use context makes stakeholder communication planning relevant. Public status updates are affirmative communication evidence, but the record does not supply the maintained plan, context-specific contact provisions and full workaround/alternative-process coverage required by MG-2.4-001. The planning outcome remains unresolved without using voluntary adoption as a gate.

conclusion_change.previous: The decisive governance failure was not merely reduced availability. The system converted one operational cause—backend availability failure—into a different user-facing state—login required. That representation could direct users toward credential or account recovery when the corrective action belonged to provider-side service recovery. Access-state integrity requires those causes and recovery routes to remain distinguishable even during overload. The published conversion of backend availability errors into login flows supports the retained access-state failure; overload alone does not. Provider root-cause attribution remains first-party reporting without independently reviewed telemetry. The reviewed external candidates retain unestablished framework undertaking and prescribed deactivation/degradation scope, so no requirement finding is asserted.
